bidayaMapping.topic: the subject and scope of philosophy
bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya defines philosophy through being qua being; Nihāya explains why demonstrative inquiry treats the existent universally.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Divine wisdom is a science that investigates the conditions of an existent insofar as it is existent. Its subject—the thing whose essential attributes are investigated—is the existent precisely as existent. Its aim is to know existents universally and to distinguish them from what has no true existence.
sourceEvidence.quote: Divine wisdom is a science that investigates the conditions of an existent insofar as it is existent.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: For this very reason, in this kind of inquiry we turn to investigating the condition of the existent universally, and thereby learn the conditions of the existent without qualification insofar as it is universal.
destinationEvidence.quote: For this very reason, in this kind of inquiry we turn to investigating the condition of the existent universally, and thereby learn the conditions of the existent without qualification insofar as it is universal.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya explains why existence cannot receive a real definition; Nihāya invokes its primary conception when explaining why philosophy needs no other science to establish its subject.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The concept of existence is self-evident: it is grasped through itself, without anything else mediating our understanding. No real definition (ḥadd) or descriptive definition (rasm) can make it known, because what makes something known must be clearer and more evident than what is made known.
sourceEvidence.quote: The concept of existence is self-evident: it is grasped through itself, without anything else mediating our understanding.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Philosophy, however, depends upon none of the sciences for establishing its own subject. Its subject is the existent in general, of which we have a primary conception and whose existence we likewise affirm primarily, because existence is its very self.
destinationEvidence.quote: Philosophy, however, depends upon none of the sciences for establishing its own subject.

bidayaMapping.topic: the univocity of the concept of existence
bidayaMapping.comparison: Both distinguish a single meaning of existence from a merely shared expression; Nihāya develops the consequences and objections.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Existence is predicated of its subjects with one meaning: the term has a common intelligible signification, not merely the same verbal sound.
sourceEvidence.quote: Existence is predicated of its subjects with one meaning: the term has a common intelligible signification, not merely the same verbal sound.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Existence, as a concept, is shared in meaning: it is predicated with one meaning of everything of which it is predicated.
destinationEvidence.quote: Existence, as a concept, is shared in meaning: it is predicated with one meaning of everything of which it is predicated.

bidayaMapping.topic: the conceptual distinction between existence and quiddity
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya places Bidāya’s three tests for the distinction within the consequences of the primacy of existence.
bidayaMapping.caution: The distinction is intellectual; it does not posit two separately existing constituents in the concrete thing.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Existence is additional to quiddity, in the sense that understanding the one is not the same as understanding the other. The intellect can abstract the quiddity—the answer to “What is it?”—consider it separately, and then attribute existence to it. This is what is meant here by the attribution of existence. Existence is therefore neither identical with quiddity nor one of its constituents.
sourceEvidence.quote: Existence is additional to quiddity, in the sense that understanding the one is not the same as understanding the other.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Sixth, existence supervenes upon quiddity. This means that the intellect can strip quiddity of existence and understand it by itself, without considering its existence. Existence is therefore neither identical with it nor part of it. Evidence for this includes the possibility of negating existence of quiddity, the need for proof that it is qualified by existence, and its equal relation in itself to existence and nonexistence. Were existence identical with quiddity or a part of it, none of these would be correct.
destinationEvidence.quote: Sixth, existence supervenes upon quiddity. This means that the intellect can strip quiddity of existence and understand it by itself, without considering its existence. Existence is therefore neither identical with it nor part of it. Evidence for this includes the possibility of negating existence of quiddity, the need for proof that it

bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya argues from quiddity’s indifference to existence; Nihāya begins from one concrete reality and distinguishes its primary and intellectually derived aspects.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Here is one demonstration. Quiddity considered simply as quiddity is indifferent to existence and nonexistence. If its emergence from that indifference into actuality, with the consequent real effects, occurred by quiddity alone rather than through existence, quiddity would turn into what it was not, an impossibility. Existence therefore brings it beyond indifference and is primary.
sourceEvidence.quote: Here is one demonstration. Quiddity considered simply as quiddity is indifferent to existence and nonexistence. If its emergence from that indifference into actuality, with the consequent real effects, occurred by quiddity alone rather than through existence, quiddity would turn into what it was not, an impossibility. Existence therefore

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity differs from existence, since what is peculiar to each differs from what is shared. Moreover, quiddity in itself does not refuse either the predication or the negation of existence. Were it identical with existence, existence could not be negated of it, since a thing cannot be negated of itself. The aspect of quiddity that we find in things therefore differs from the aspect of existence that we find in them. Since each of these things has only one reality, one of these two aspects—quiddity and existence—corresponds to its reality and actuality. This is what is meant by primacy. The other aspect is intellectually derived from the primary aspect, and reality is attributed to it incidentally.
destinationEvidence.quote: Quiddity differs from existence, since what is peculiar to each differs from what is shared.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya states that degrees differ through the reality they share; Nihāya distinguishes existential divisions from incidental quiddative multiplicity.
bidayaMapping.caution: The gradation concerns existence itself, not an intrinsic increase or decrease in a quiddity’s defining content.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Likewise, existence is a single reality with different ranks distinguished by intensity and weakness, priority and posteriority, and other such respects. The very respect in which its degrees differ is the respect in which they are united. A degree's distinguishing character is neither an essential component superadded to existence, since existence is simple, nor something extraneous to existence, since the doctrine of primacy denies that another independently real principle stands outside it. Each degree has its own intrinsic determination.
sourceEvidence.quote: Likewise, existence is a single reality with different ranks distinguished by intensity and weakness, priority and posteriority, and other such respects.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Multiplicity in the second respect, however, is what belongs to existence through the divisions that occur in existence itself, such as its division into necessary and contingent, one and many, actual and potential, and the like. It was established in the preceding chapter that existence is simple and that there is nothing other than it.
destinationEvidence.quote: Multiplicity in the second respect, however, is what belongs to existence through the divisions that occur in existence itself, such as its division into necessary and contingent, one and many, actual and potential, and the like.

bidayaMapping.topic: the determination of existence through quiddities
bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya distinguishes ways existence is particularised and explains predication of existence; Nihāya explains quiddities as modes and limits of the one concrete actuality.
bidayaMapping.caution: This is a dispersed development within the primacy chapter, not a separate chapter with the same title.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The ‘accruing’ (ʿurūḍ) of existence to a quiddity, and its being established for that quiddity, is not an instance of categorial inherence in which an accident requires its subject to be already actual. Rather, for existence to obtain for a quiddity is precisely for that quiddity to obtain *through existence*. This is what follows from the primacy of existence and the derivative status of quiddity. The intellect, accustomed to speaking in terms of quiddities, takes the quiddity as the grammatical subject and predicates existence of it, whereas the underlying ontological dependence runs in the opposite direction.
sourceEvidence.quote: The ‘accruing’ (ʿurūḍ) of existence to a quiddity, and its being established for that quiddity, is not an instance of categorial inherence in which an accident requires its subject to be already actual.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: As you have learned, this difference is intellectual; it does not conflict with the unity of quiddity and existence externally and mentally. There is only one reality, namely existence, because existence is primary and quiddity derivative. Different quiddities differentiate existence in a certain way, without anything being added to existence. This is the meaning of their statement, “Quiddities are modes of existence.” The distinction, separation, and difference in effects among existent quiddities reduce to this difference; this is the meaning of their statement, “Quiddities are the limits of existence.” The essence of each existent quiddity is a limit that its existence does not exceed. This entails negations equal in number to the existent quiddities outside it. The existent quiddity of a human, for example, is a limit of that human's existence, which does not pass beyond it to another: the human is not a horse, not a cow, not a tree, not a stone, and so on through the existent quiddities distinct from the human.
destinationEvidence.quote: As you have learned, this difference is intellectual; it does not conflict with the unity of quiddity and existence externally and mentally.

bidayaMapping.topic: the exclusion of existence from the categories and five predicables
bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya’s negative properties of existence receive a detailed account in Nihāya’s distinction between concrete existence and quiddative classifications.
bidayaMapping.caution: The concept of existence can still be universal; the denial concerns concrete existence as such.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Third, existence is neither substance nor accident. Substance is a *quiddity* which, when it exists externally, exists not in a subject. But existence is not a quiddity. An accident depends in its existence upon a subject; existence, by contrast, obtains through its own reality, and everything else is established through it.
sourceEvidence.quote: Third, existence is neither substance nor accident.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Second, existence is not qualified by any of the determinations of quiddity, such as universality and particularity; being a genus, species, differentia, proprium, or common accident; or substantiality, quantity, quality, and the other accidental categories. All these determinations supervene upon quiddity either insofar as it applies to and is true of something—as “human” applies to and is true of Zayd, ʿAmr, and the other individuals—or insofar as it falls under something, as individuals fall under species and species under genera. Existence, which is intrinsically concrete reality, admits neither application to something nor inclusion under something, neither truth of something nor predication, nor anything resembling these meanings. The concept of existence does, however, admit being true of many and being shared, like other concepts.
destinationEvidence.quote: Second, existence is not qualified by any of the determinations of quiddity, such as universality and particularity; being a genus, species, differentia, proprium, or common accident; or substantiality, quantity, quality, and the other accidental categories.

bidayaMapping.topic: nafs al-amr and the truth of propositions
bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya introduces the domain to which true propositions conform; Nihāya derives its extension beyond straightforward external and mental instances.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The broad kind of establishment embracing existence, quiddity, and these intellectual concepts is called *nafs al-amr*—‘the fact of the matter’ or what actually obtains in the relevant order. The truth of a proposition is measured by its correspondence to this. Hence we say that something is thus-and-so *in nafs al-amr*.
sourceEvidence.quote: The broad kind of establishment embracing existence, quiddity, and these intellectual concepts is called *nafs al-amr*—‘the fact of the matter’ or what actually obtains in the relevant order.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The domain that the intellect supposes for establishment and realization without qualification in this last sense is what we call “the order of things themselves.” It encompasses true mental and external propositions and what the intellect affirms without a corresponding object mentally or externally. Matters belonging to this order are, however, intellectual concomitants of quiddities, established through their establishment.
destinationEvidence.quote: The domain that the intellect supposes for establishment and realization without qualification in this last sense is what we call “the order of things themselves.” It encompasses true mental and external propositions and what the intellect affirms without a corresponding object mentally or externally.

bidayaMapping.topic: the coextension of thingness and existence
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya locates Bidāya’s rejection of thingness for the nonexistent among the consequences of the primacy of existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Thingness (*shayʾiyya*) is coextensive with existence. Non-being has no thingness, for it is sheer nullity without any positive establishment. In this sense, affirmation or establishment stands with existence, negation with non-existence.
sourceEvidence.quote: Thingness (*shayʾiyya*) is coextensive with existence.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Eighth, thingness is coextensive with existence. What has no existence has no thingness; the nonexistent, insofar as it is nonexistent, is not a thing.
destinationEvidence.quote: Eighth, thingness is coextensive with existence.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both explain why the absence of a cause is said to cause the absence of an effect only through the underlying dependence between the existents.
bidayaMapping.caution: The phrase does not give nonexistence positive causal efficacy.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Nor can non-being properly act as a cause, since it has no reality or thingness. The familiar expression ‘the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect’ is therefore approximate or figurative. Saying ‘there were no clouds, so there was no rain’ really means that the causal relation between the existence of clouds and the occurrence of rain was not realised.
sourceEvidence.quote: Nor can non-being properly act as a cause, since it has no reality or thingness.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: In this way the intellect attributes causality and being an effect to nonexistence, corresponding to what existence possesses in this respect. Thus it is said, “The nonexistence of the cause is a cause of the nonexistence of the effect.” Here nonexistence is related to the cause and the effect, and the two nonexistences become differentiated. The nonexistence of the effect is then made dependent on the nonexistence of the cause, just as the existence of the effect depended on the existence of the cause. This is a kind of figurative expression whose actual significance is to indicate the dependence obtaining between the two existences.
destinationEvidence.quote: In this way the intellect attributes causality and being an effect to nonexistence, corresponding to what existence possesses in this respect.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya resolves the same apparent self-contradiction by distinguishing sheer nullity from its mentally established concept.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: An objection says that the proposition ‘Absolute non-existence cannot be spoken of’ contradicts itself: the statement appears to speak *about* the very thing declared unspeakable. The answer requires the distinction between two modes of predication, taken up later under unity and multiplicity.
sourceEvidence.quote: An objection says that the proposition ‘Absolute non-existence cannot be spoken of’ contradicts itself: the statement appears to speak *about* the very thing declared unspeakable.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The answer is that nothing can be asserted of the absolutely nonexistent insofar as it is sheer nullity in reality. But insofar as its concept has a certain mental subsistence, it can be asserted of it that nothing can be asserted of it. The respects are therefore different.
destinationEvidence.quote: The answer is that nothing can be asserted of the absolutely nonexistent insofar as it is sheer nullity in reality.

bidayaMapping.topic: the impossibility of numerical restoration after annihilation
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya derives Bidāya’s restoration problem from the impossibility of repeating one numerical existence.
bidayaMapping.caution: The claim concerns numerical identity after complete annihilation; the chapter separately distinguishes resurrection as transition between modes of being.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The philosophers maintain that the numerical restoration of the very same thing after its complete annihilation is impossible. Some theologians agree; most theologians, as reported here, consider it possible. Avicenna regarded its impossibility as evident: since the non-existent has no thingness, there is no subject of restoration while it is non-existent.
sourceEvidence.quote: The philosophers maintain that the numerical restoration of the very same thing after its complete annihilation is impossible.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: This established impossibility of the repetition of a thing's existence with intervening nonexistence is what is meant by their statement, “Restoring the nonexistent as numerically the same thing is impossible.” The Shaykh regarded the impossibility of restoring the nonexistent as numerically the same thing as self-evident.
destinationEvidence.quote: This established impossibility of the repetition of a thing's existence with intervening nonexistence is what is meant by their statement, “Restoring the nonexistent as numerically the same thing is impossible.” The Shaykh regarded the impossibility of restoring the nonexistent as numerically the same thing as self-evident.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both preserve quiddative content while distinguishing the effects of external existence from the effects of a cognition; Nihāya develops the objections and replies.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The prevailing position among philosophers is that quiddities have, in addition to their external existence—where their characteristic effects follow from them—another mode of existence in which those effects do not follow. This is called *mental existence* (al-wujūd al-dhihnī). A human being existing outside the mind is a substance, existing not in a subject; insofar as the human is a body, three dimensions can be supposed in it; and insofar as it is a living and rational being, it possesses vegetative, animal, and rational faculties. The effects associated with these genera, differentiae, and properties are manifest externally. The human being as known in the mind, however, is human in its essential character and possesses the same definition, but none of those external effects follow from it.
sourceEvidence.quote: The prevailing position among philosophers is that quiddities have, in addition to their external existence—where their characteristic effects follow from them—another mode of existence in which those effects do not follow.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The well-known position of the philosophers is that these quiddities which exist externally and upon which their effects follow have another existence in which those very external effects do not follow upon them, although other effects, different from their external effects, do follow upon them.
destinationEvidence.quote: The well-known position of the philosophers is that these quiddities which exist externally and upon which their effects follow have another existence in which those very external effects do not follow upon them, although other effects, different from their external effects, do follow upon them.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the same argument from the connection in a true proposition to a dependent mode of existence.
bidayaMapping.caution: The connective is not a third self-standing entity inserted between the terms.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The being of the connection is constituted in its terms. It is neither extraneous nor independent of them in any respect, and has no self-contained conceptual signification. We call it *linking existence* (al-wujūd al-rābiṭ). By contrast, the being of subject and predicate admits an independently meaningful concept; this is *predicative existence* (al-wujūd al-maḥmūlī), or independent existence. Existence is thus divided into independent and linking modes.
sourceEvidence.quote: The being of the connection is constituted in its terms.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: This is because there are propositions about external reality whose subjects and predicates apply to external reality, such as “Zayd is standing” and “The human being laughs.” There are also qualifying compounds drawn from these propositions, such as “Zayd’s standing” and “the human being’s laughter.” Between their terms we find something that we call a relation or connection. We do not find it in the subject alone, in the predicate alone, between the subject and something other than the predicate, or between the predicate and something other than the subject. There is, therefore, something existent in addition to the subject and predicate.
destinationEvidence.quote: This is because there are propositions about external reality whose subjects and predicates apply to external reality, such as “Zayd is standing” and “The human being laughs.” There are also qualifying compounds drawn from these propositions, such as “Zayd’s standing” and “the human being’s laughter.” Between their

bidayaMapping.topic: the consideration of an effect as connective or independent
bidayaMapping.comparison: Both argue that an effect is dependent in relation to its cause while allowing an independently meaningful concept when considered in itself.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The author takes the opposite view. As will be shown in the stage on cause and effect, the existences of effects are linking existences in relation to their causes. But effects include substances and accidents, and these possess predicative existences whose concepts are independently meaningful. The very same existent is therefore linking in relation to its cause and independently predicable when considered in itself. Its mode of consideration differs according to the relation in which it is taken.
sourceEvidence.quote: The author takes the opposite view. As will be shown in the stage on cause and effect, the existences of effects are linking existences in relation to their causes. But effects include substances and accidents, and these possess predicative existences whose concepts are independently meaningful. The very same existent is therefore

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Is the difference between independent and connective existence a difference in kind, or is it not? That is, can connective existence, which has a dependent meaning, shed this character and become an independent meaning when attention is directed to it independently, after having had the meaning of a particle, or can it not? The correct position is the latter alternative: the difference is not one of kind. For, as will be explained in the discussions of cause and effect, an effect’s need for its cause is rooted in its very essence. This entails that it is need itself and that its essence subsists through the existence of the cause, having no independence apart from it in any respect. It follows that the existence of every effect—whether it is a substance or an accident—is connective when considered in relation to its cause, although, when considered in itself and when such effects are compared with one another, it is a substance or an accident existing in itself. Thus the difference between connective and independent existence is not a difference in kind such that the nonindependent concept abstracted from the connective could not be transformed into the independent concept abstracted from the independent.
destinationEvidence.quote: Is the difference between independent and connective existence a difference in kind, or is it not?

bidayaMapping.comparison: Knowledge’s removal of ignorance illustrates how one existence both actualises its own quiddity and perfects its subject.
bidayaMapping.caution: Existence for another is distinct from the pure connective that has no independent conceptual content.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: For example, knowledge actualises its own quiddity as a quality and, by that very existence, removes ignorance from the soul in which it occurs. Power similarly actualises its own quiddity while removing incapacity from the subject that possesses it.
sourceEvidence.quote: For example, knowledge actualises its own quiddity as a quality and, by that very existence, removes ignorance from the soul in which it occurs.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: By a thing’s existence being for another, we mean that its existence in itself—the existence that excludes nonexistence from its quiddity—is itself also what excludes nonexistence from something else. It does not exclude the nonexistence of that other thing’s quiddity and essence, for otherwise a single existent would have two quiddities, which is impossible. Rather, it excludes a nonexistence additional to that other thing’s quiddity and essence and having a certain concomitance with it. Knowledge, for example, by its existence excludes nonexistence from its own quiddity, while that very same existence excludes ignorance, which is a certain nonexistence, from its subject.
destinationEvidence.quote: By a thing’s existence being for another, we mean that its existence in itself—the existence that excludes nonexistence from its quiddity—is itself also what excludes nonexistence from something else.

bidayaMapping.topic: the exhaustive threefold division of modality
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya formalises the same division into necessary, impossible, and possible through necessity and its negation.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Whenever a concept is considered in relation to existence, one of three alternatives must hold. Existence is necessary for it, and it is therefore *necessary*; or existence is impossible for it, and it is *impossible*; or neither its existence nor its non-existence is necessary, and it is *possible* or *contingent*.
sourceEvidence.quote: Whenever a concept is considered in relation to existence, one of three alternatives must hold.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Whatever concept we suppose and then relate existence to, either existence belongs to it necessarily, which is necessity; or existence is necessarily excluded from it—that is, nonexistence belongs to it necessarily—which is impossibility; or neither existence nor nonexistence belongs to it necessarily, which is possibility.
destinationEvidence.quote: Whatever concept we suppose and then relate existence to, either existence belongs to it necessarily, which is necessity; or existence is necessarily excluded from it—that is, nonexistence belongs to it necessarily—which is impossibility; or neither existence nor nonexistence belongs to it necessarily, which is possibility.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya spells out the difference between modality through another and modality considered relative to another, preserving the exclusion of possibility through another.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Each of the three modalities is further distinguished as intrinsic, through another, or relative to another—except that *possibility through another* is not admitted. Intrinsic modality belongs to a thing from the very supposition of what it is, apart from anything else. Modality through another depends upon something different from the thing, while modality relative to another appears when the thing is compared with that other.
sourceEvidence.quote: Each of the three modalities is further distinguished as intrinsic, through another, or relative to another—except that *possibility through another* is not admitted.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: By “intrinsic” is meant that positing the essence, while disregarding everything other than it, suffices for its characterization by the modality. “Through another” means that positing it in this way does not suffice; rather, the characterization depends on another’s bestowal and necessitation. “Relative to another” means that the characterization is considered in relation to another, in virtue of a requirement on its part, “requirement” here being broader than causal necessitation.
destinationEvidence.quote: By “intrinsic” is meant that positing the essence, while disregarding everything other than it, suffices for its characterization by the modality.

bidayaMapping.topic: the absence of an additional quiddity in the Necessary
bidayaMapping.comparison: Both explain the formula that the Necessary’s quiddity is its existence as denying a quiddity beyond its proper existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: In the Necessary Existent, quiddity is identical with existence. This means that He has no quiddity or essence over and above His particular existence.
sourceEvidence.quote: In the Necessary Existent, quiddity is identical with existence.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The quiddity of the intrinsically necessary existent is its existence: that is, it has no quiddity beyond the existence proper to it.
destinationEvidence.quote: The quiddity of the intrinsically necessary existent is its existence: that is, it has no quiddity beyond the existence proper to it.

bidayaMapping.topic: the necessity of every possible divine perfection
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the claim that no aspect of unactualised possibility can belong to the Necessary.
bidayaMapping.caution: Possible here includes general possibility: the absence of impossibility, not contingent openness to either alternative.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The Necessary Existent is necessary in every respect. Suppose there were a perfection which could belong to Him in the broad sense of possibility but did not belong to Him necessarily. He would then have an aspect of possibility in relation to that perfection, lacking it in His own reality and standing equally open to its possession or absence.
sourceEvidence.quote: The Necessary Existent is necessary in every respect.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn, may God have mercy upon him, said: “What is meant by this is that there is no aspect of possibility in the Necessary Existent. Everything that is possible for it in the sense of general possibility is necessary for it.
destinationEvidence.quote: Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn, may God have mercy upon him, said: “What is meant by this is that there is no aspect of possibility in the Necessary Existent.

bidayaMapping.topic: causal necessitation and the rejection of mere preponderance
bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya introduces the dispute over whether a cause must necessitate its effect; Nihāya states why merely favouring existence leaves the causal question unanswered.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: A contingent thing, considered in itself, is equally related to existence and non-existence. Its existence therefore depends on something called a cause, and its non-existence upon the absence of the cause. Must the cause make the effect's existence *necessary*—the necessity which comes through another—or is it sufficient that one alternative merely acquire a greater preponderance even without attaining necessity? The same question can be asked of non-existence.
sourceEvidence.quote: A contingent thing, considered in itself, is equally related to existence and non-existence.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The cause's giving preponderance to the side of existence can only be its making existence necessary. Without this necessitation, existence would not be determined for the quiddity: either alternative would remain admissible, and the question would remain, “Why did it become existent when nonexistence was admissible for it?” A cause's bringing something into existence is therefore not complete unless it first makes existence necessary for the effect.
destinationEvidence.quote: The cause's giving preponderance to the side of existence can only be its making existence necessary.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya expands Bidāya’s distinction between special and general possibility and separates further uses of the term.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The term “possibility” is also used more generally to exclude necessity on the *opposite* side, whether the side affirmed is necessary or not. Thus one says “This is possible” to mean “This is not impossible.” This is broader than special possibility and is called *general possibility* (al-imkān al-ʿāmm), as in ordinary speech.
sourceEvidence.quote: The term “possibility” is also used more generally to exclude necessity on the *opposite* side, whether the side affirmed is necessary or not.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Possibility in this sense is broader in its range of cases than possibility in the preceding sense—that is, the negation of the two necessities—and than either necessity or impossibility. It is not broader conceptually, since there is no common concept uniting the modalities. The philosophers then transferred the term specifically to the negation of necessity on both sides. They called this “special possibility” or “possibility in the special sense,” and called ordinary usage “general possibility” or “possibility in the general sense.”
destinationEvidence.quote: Possibility in this sense is broader in its range of cases than possibility in the preceding sense—that is, the negation of the two necessities—and than either necessity or impossibility.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya clarifies how possibility is intellectually predicated while its subject is qualified by it externally.
bidayaMapping.caution: An intellectual consideration is not thereby a groundless fiction; Nihāya expressly denies both a separate external entity and a wholly ungrounded consideration.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Intrinsic possibility is an *intellectual consideration* because it belongs to a quiddity considered by the intellect apart from its existence and non-existence. The quiddity, taken in precisely that abstract fashion, is itself an object of intellectual consideration; what belongs to it under that consideration is likewise intellectually considered.
sourceEvidence.quote: Intrinsic possibility is an *intellectual consideration* because it belongs to a quiddity considered by the intellect apart from its existence and non-existence.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The answer is that qualification by an attribute among concrete things does not require that attribute to be realized among them through a separate, independent existence. It is enough for it to exist through the existence of what it qualifies. Possibility is one of the secondary philosophical intelligibles: its occurrence as a predicate is in the mind, while qualification by it is external, and such intelligibles exist externally through the existence of their subjects.
destinationEvidence.quote: The answer is that qualification by an attribute among concrete things does not require that attribute to be realized among them through a separate, independent existence.

bidayaMapping.topic: contingency as the ground of causal need
bidayaMapping.comparison: Both argue from a quiddity’s equal relation to existence and nonexistence, before comparing contingency with temporal origination.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: That a contingent being needs a cause is one of the primary necessities of thought: merely conceiving the subject and predicate suffices for assent. If one understands a contingent quiddity as equally related to existence and non-existence, and recognises that departing from such equality requires something beyond the quiddity to determine one alternative, one assents immediately that it must depend on a cause.
sourceEvidence.quote: That a contingent being needs a cause is one of the primary necessities of thought: merely conceiving the subject and predicate suffices for assent.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The possible existent’s need for something beyond its quiddity—that is, its dependence upon such a thing in acquiring existence or nonexistence—is among the primary self-evident truths. Assent to it requires no more than conceiving its subject and predicate. For when we conceive a quiddity as possible, equally related to existence and nonexistence, and conceive the preponderance of either side for it and its acquisition of that side as dependent upon something beyond the quiddity, we assent to this without delay. Thus, the possible existent’s being characterized by either of the two attributes, existence and nonexistence, depends upon something beyond itself, which we call the “cause.” No sound intellect doubts this.
destinationEvidence.quote: The possible existent’s need for something beyond its quiddity—that is, its dependence upon such a thing in acquiring existence or nonexistence—is among the primary self-evident truths.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops Bidāya’s argument that an effect’s connective existence cannot become independent after origination.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: A second argument is that an effect's existence is *linking existence*, as previously indicated and as the discussion of causality will explain further. Its existence depends upon the cause as part of what it is: it does not subsist independently. Consequently, its need for the cause is the same in origination and continuance.
sourceEvidence.quote: A second argument is that an effect's existence is *linking existence*, as previously indicated and as the discussion of causality will explain further.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Another argument: the concrete identity of each thing is its own particular existence, while quiddity is derivative and abstracted from it, as explained earlier. The existence of the possible effect is a connective existence, dependent in its very essence upon its cause and constituted through it. It has no independence apart from the cause and never sheds this condition, as will be explained, God willing. Its condition with respect to needing a cause is therefore the same in origination and continuance, and need is inseparable from it.
destinationEvidence.quote: Another argument: the concrete identity of each thing is its own particular existence, while quiddity is derivative and abstracted from it, as explained earlier.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya makes explicit the difference between excluding existence and nonexistence from a definition and excluding both from reality.
bidayaMapping.caution: The exclusion from the rank of quiddity does not suspend the principle of noncontradiction.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity as such is nothing but itself: it is neither existent nor non-existent, nor anything else added to its defining account. This is the meaning of the philosophers' statement that contradictories are both excluded from the *rank of quiddity*. They mean that neither opposite is included in what constitutes the quiddity, not that a thing in reality can be without both members of a contradictory pair.
sourceEvidence.quote: Quiddity as such is nothing but itself: it is neither existent nor non-existent, nor anything else added to its defining account.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity (māhiyya), which is “what is said in answer to the question ‘What is it?’,” does not, considered as such and with regard to its own essence, preclude being characterized as existent or nonexistent. It is therefore, in its own essence, neither existent nor nonexistent. This means that neither existence nor nonexistence is included in its own essence, whether as identical with it or as a part of it, although in reality it is invariably characterized by one of them, in the manner of being characterized by an attribute extrinsic to the essence. In other words, quiddity is neither existent nor nonexistent by primary predication, although by common predication it is either existent or nonexistent. This is what they mean when they say: “The exclusion of existence and nonexistence from quiddity considered as such is the exclusion of two contradictories from a particular level. This is not impossible; what is impossible is their exclusion from reality absolutely and at all its levels.” Their meaning is that the contradictory of existence included in the essence is not nonexistence included in the essence. Rather, it is the negation of existence included in the essence: “included in the essence,” which specifies the level, qualifies the existence, not its negation. That is, it is the negation of what is qualified, not a qualified negation.
destinationEvidence.quote: Quiddity (māhiyya), which is “what is said in answer to the question ‘What is it?’,” does not, considered as such and with regard to its own essence, preclude being characterized as existent or nonexistent.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both distinguish consideration with something, with exclusion, and without condition; the expanded account explains their philosophical use.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: A quiddity can be considered in three ways with respect to what may be added to it. It may be taken *with the condition of something* (bi-sharṭ shayʾ), *with the condition of nothing else* (bi-sharṭ lā), or *without such a condition* (lā bi-sharṭ). These alternatives exhaust the possibilities of consideration.
sourceEvidence.quote: A quiddity can be considered in three ways with respect to what may be added to it.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity admits of three ways of being considered in relation to the particular features that accompany it: it may be taken subject to the condition of something, subject to the condition of exclusion, or without condition. This division is exhaustive.
destinationEvidence.quote: Quiddity admits of three ways of being considered in relation to the particular features that accompany it: it may be taken subject to the condition of something, subject to the condition of exclusion, or without condition.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both identify essential predicates through inclusion in a quiddity’s defining account; the expanded account develops the contrast with accidental predicates.
bidayaMapping.caution: Accidental predication in this sense is broader than belonging to an ontological accidental category.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The intelligible meanings included in a quiddity's definition, such that removal of any one would remove that quiddity, are called its *essential constituents* (dhātiyyāt). Predicates outside this defining account are *accidental* (ʿaraḍiyyāt).
sourceEvidence.quote: The intelligible meanings included in a quiddity's definition, such that removal of any one would remove that quiddity, are called its *essential constituents* (dhātiyyāt).

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The concepts taken into account in quiddities—those included in their definitions, with whose removal the quiddities themselves are removed—are called “essential predicates.”
destinationEvidence.quote: The concepts taken into account in quiddities—those included in their definitions, with whose removal the quiddities themselves are removed—are called “essential predicates.”

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya explicitly draws on the logical classification introduced in Bidāya before developing the ontological relations among the constituents.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Some essential meanings occur in several species, while others are particular to one. Animality, for example, is common to humans, horses, and other species. Rationality is specific to human being. The common essential constituent is called *genus* (jins), and the specific determining constituent *differentia* (faṣl). Genus and differentia are divided into proximate and remote, and genera and species can be arranged as highest, intermediate, or lowest. Logic examines these classifications in detail.
sourceEvidence.quote: Some essential meanings occur in several species, while others are particular to one.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: It has been explained in logic that some of the essential meanings of species included in their definitions are shared by more than one species, such as animal, which is shared by human being, horse, and others. Other such meanings belong exclusively to one species, such as rational, which belongs exclusively to human being. The shared part is called a “genus,” and the exclusive part is called a “differentia.”
destinationEvidence.quote: It has been explained in logic that some of the essential meanings of species included in their definitions are shared by more than one species, such as animal, which is shared by human being, horse, and others.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both caution that a familiar feature used as a logical differentia may substitute for a species’ difficult-to-know real constituent.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The logical differentia is the most distinctive and best-known concomitant belonging to a species. It is placed in definitions in the position of the real differentia because discovering the true constituent which makes a species what it is is often difficult.
sourceEvidence.quote: The logical differentia is the most distinctive and best-known concomitant belonging to a species.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The first is the most specific and best known of the concomitants that accrue to a species. Such a concomitant is counted as a differentia and placed in definitions in the position of real differentiae only because it is difficult to obtain the real differentiae that constitute species, or because the language contains no name that denotes them by complete correspondence. An example is “rational” (nāṭiq), taken as the differentia of the human being. What is meant by nuṭq is either speaking, which in one respect belongs to audible qualities, or apprehending universals, which they class among qualities of the soul. Quality of whatever kind is an accident, and accidents do not constitute substances. This is called a “logical differentia.”
destinationEvidence.quote: The first is the most specific and best known of the concomitants that accrue to a species.

bidayaMapping.topic: real composition and the unity of species
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops Bidāya’s distinction between a genuinely unified composite with new effects and an aggregate such as an army or house.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: A genuine composite is distinguished from a mere aggregate by its true unity. When two constituents are combined, a third actuality results that differs from either constituent taken alone and has properties not reducible to their individual properties. A mineral substance, for example, has properties other than those of the elements composing it. This contrasts with an army, which is a plurality of soldiers, or a building, an arrangement of bricks, plaster, and other components. The author therefore favours the thesis that the composition of matter and form is a unity of actualisation, not merely the juxtaposition of two completed things.
sourceEvidence.quote: A genuine composite is distinguished from a mere aggregate by its true unity.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: A real composite is distinguished from other composites by real unity. Through the composition of its parts, something else arises beyond them, having a new, distinctive effect beyond the effects of the parts. It is unlike composites existing only by consideration, which have no effect beyond the effects of their parts, such as an army composed of individuals or a house composed of bricks, plaster, and other things.
destinationEvidence.quote: A real composite is distinguished from other composites by real unity.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both reject the claim that universality is merely indistinct perception and locate universality in the mental mode of quiddity.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: But if universality were only this weakness of discrimination, a universal concept such as ‘human’ could not truly be predicated of more than one of its individual instances. Likewise, universal laws applying to indefinitely many cases, such as ‘four is even’ or ‘every contingent existent has a cause of its existence’, would be true of at most one case and false of the others. Direct intellectual awareness rejects this result.
sourceEvidence.quote: But if universality were only this weakness of discrimination, a universal concept such as ‘human’ could not truly be predicated of more than one of its individual instances.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: This is unsound. If things were so, the instance of quiddity would in reality be only one of its individuals, and universal propositions would be false, such as “Every possible existent has a cause,” “Every four is even,” and “Every multiplicity is composed of units.” Self-evident judgment rejects this. The truth, then, is that universality and particularity are concomitants of the existence of quiddities: universality belongs to their mental existence, and particularity to their external existence.
destinationEvidence.quote: This is unsound. If things were so, the instance of quiddity would in reality be only one of its individuals, and universal propositions would be false, such as “Every possible existent has a cause,” “Every four is even,” and “Every multiplicity is composed of units.” Self-evident judgment rejects this. The truth, then, is that

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya’s discussion of individuation explains why adding universal differentiations does not yield individuality, which belongs to existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: To distinguish one quiddity from another is to mark their difference so that they are not predicable of one another. Human being is distinguished from horse, for example, by the possession of rationality. *Individuation* (tashakhkhuṣ), by contrast, is the determination of a quiddity in such a way that it cannot be predicated of many, as with the individual human being Zayd.
sourceEvidence.quote: To distinguish one quiddity from another is to mark their difference so that they are not predicable of one another.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: “What individuates a thing—in the sense of that through which it becomes incapable of being shared—is in reality nothing other than that thing’s existence itself, as the Second Teacher held. Every existence is individuated through its own essence. If the particular mode of a thing’s existence is disregarded, the intellect does not refuse to allow it to be shared, even if a thousand specifying features are added to it. For distinction in reality differs from individuation: the former belongs to a thing in comparison with those things that share something general with it, whereas the latter belongs to it considered in itself. Indeed, if it had nothing sharing something with it, it would not need an additional distinguishing feature, even though it would possess individuation in itself. It is not implausible that distinction should bring about a thing’s preparedness for individuation. For, in the case of a material species dispersed among individuals, unless matter has acquired a disposition specifically for one of them, that individual’s existence does not emanate from the highest principle.” End of quotation.
destinationEvidence.quote: “What individuates a thing—in the sense of that through which it becomes incapable of being shared—is in reality nothing other than that thing’s existence itself, as the Second Teacher held.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both classify quiddities by whether their external existence is in a subject independent of them.
bidayaMapping.caution: This is a description through an existential concomitant, not a definition of a highest genus by a still higher genus.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity is divided at the outset into *substance* and *accident*. A quiddity is substantial if, when existing outside the mind, it exists not in a subject that could subsist independently of it. It may exist without inhering in any subject at all, as a self-subsistent intellectual substance does; or it may exist in something that cannot itself exist without it, as a substantial elemental form exists in matter that is actualised through the form.
sourceEvidence.quote: Quiddity is divided at the outset into *substance* and *accident*.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Quiddity divides primarily into a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists not in a subject independent of it—this is the quiddity of substance—and a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists in a subject independent of it—these are the nine accidental categories.
destinationEvidence.quote: Quiddity divides primarily into a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists not in a subject independent of it—this is the quiddity of substance—and a quiddity which, when it exists externally, exists in a subject independent of it—these are the nine accidental categories.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya qualifies the same fivefold division by explaining its inductive basis and why its form is not an exhaustive a priori division.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Substances are conventionally divided into five kinds: matter, form, body, soul, and intellect. This division is based, in reality, on induction from the substantial kinds whose existence has been argued for.
sourceEvidence.quote: Substances are conventionally divided into five kinds: matter, form, body, soul, and intellect.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: This is not an intellectual division turning upon affirmation and negation. A substance composed of an inhering substance and a substance serving as substrate is not, as a matter of intellectual possibility, confined to body. It is possible that existence includes a material substance composed of matter and a form other than corporeal form. Their restriction of the primary material species to body rests instead upon their induction. Moreover, you have already learned that substantial form does not fall under the category of substance, although “substance” applies to it as an extrinsic concomitant.
destinationEvidence.quote: This is not an intellectual division turning upon affirmation and negation.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both begin from corporeal extension and then investigate continuity and the competing accounts of bodily parts.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Bodies plainly differ from one another while sharing *corporeality*, the character of a substance extended in three dimensions. A body as body is divisible in its possible dimensions and appears to sense as a connected unity.
sourceEvidence.quote: Bodies plainly differ from one another while sharing *corporeality*, the character of a substance extended in three dimensions.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: There is no doubt that body exists, in the sense of a substance in which three lines intersecting at right angles can be posited, even if they are not actually present in it, as in a sphere or a cylinder.
destinationEvidence.quote: There is no doubt that body exists, in the sense of a substance in which three lines intersecting at right angles can be posited, even if they are not actually present in it, as in a sphere or a cylinder.

bidayaMapping.topic: matter and form through potentiality and actuality
bidayaMapping.comparison: Both distinguish the actuality of corporeal extension from the receptivity to further forms and perfections.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Body considered simply as body—that in which corporeal extension first arises in its own right—is actual. Yet insofar as specific substantial forms and their concomitant determinations can come to it, it is potential. The respect of actuality differs from the respect of potentiality: actuality is constituted by possession, while potentiality is constituted by lack or receptivity.
sourceEvidence.quote: Body considered simply as body—that in which corporeal extension first arises in its own right—is actual.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: There is no doubt that body, insofar as it is a substance in which the three dimensions can be posited, is something actual. Insofar as other primary perfections called specific forms, which perfect its substance, and secondary perfections consisting of accidents outside its substance can exist in it, it is something potential.
destinationEvidence.quote: There is no doubt that body, insofar as it is a substance in which the three dimensions can be posited, is something actual.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya argues from diverse bodily effects; Nihāya explains the constitutive status of the forms that differentiate bodily species.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: The different actions therefore require different principles. If these were only distinct accidents, those accidents would ultimately have to depend upon correspondingly distinct substantial realities. The distinct principles cannot simply be corporeality itself, since this is common to all bodies. They are substantial principles through which bodies are constituted as different kinds, called *specific substantial forms* (al-ṣuwar al-nawʿiyya).
sourceEvidence.quote: The different actions therefore require different principles.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: We find differences among bodies in respect of concepts that apply to them, whose belonging to them is self-evident and which cannot be separated from them. We cannot conceive a body without conceiving it, for example, as an element, a mineral compound, a tree, an animal, and so on. Body's qualification by these concepts in this manner indicates that they are among its constituents. Since each is more particular than body, they constitute the substance of its essence, and a species of body results through the addition of each to it. Only a substance can constitute a substance. These, therefore, are substantial forms that differentiate body into species.
destinationEvidence.quote: We find differences among bodies in respect of concepts that apply to them, whose belonging to them is self-evident and which cannot be separated from them.

bidayaMapping.topic: the inseparability of matter and form
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya expands the argument that pure receptivity requires an actual form for determinate existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Prime matter cannot be stripped of all form, because its nature is to be potential in every respect. It cannot exist except by being constituted through a substantial actuality united with it. Nothing exists without actuality, and the actual substantial principle that fulfils this role is form. Prime matter therefore cannot exist independently of form.
sourceEvidence.quote: Prime matter cannot be stripped of all form, because its nature is to be potential in every respect.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Matter cannot be stripped of form because, in its very essence and substance, it is the potentiality for things. Its only share of actuality is the actuality of having no actuality. Existence necessarily accompanies actuality as opposed to potentiality. In its existence, therefore, matter needs an actual existent with determinate existence, with which it unites and through whose determinacy it becomes determinate. This is what is called “form.”
destinationEvidence.quote: Matter cannot be stripped of form because, in its very essence and substance, it is the potentiality for things.

bidayaMapping.topic: the asymmetric dependence of matter and form
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya distinguishes form as a co-cause of matter’s determinate existence from matter as the receptive constituent of a composite.
bidayaMapping.caution: The dependence is in different respects; it is not a vicious circle of two complete efficient causes.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Matter and form depend upon one another. This follows generally from their forming a genuinely unified composite, since the constituents of a true composite need one another. More specifically, form needs matter for its *determination as a specific kind*: its occurrence requires a prior disposition borne by matter, which was previously joined to another form, and so on.
sourceEvidence.quote: Matter and form depend upon one another. This follows generally from their forming a genuinely unified composite, since the constituents of a true composite need one another. More specifically, form needs matter for its *determination as a specific kind*: its occurrence requires a prior disposition borne by matter, which was previously

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Form in relation to matter, however, is not its formal cause. Matter is not composed of form and something else, with an intrinsic need for form. Rather, it needs form for its determinate realization, which lies outside its essence. For this reason, form is a co-cause in relation to matter and gives it determinate realization, as explained above.
destinationEvidence.quote: Form in relation to matter, however, is not its formal cause.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya separates the definition, divisions, and properties of quantity into several chapters; this passage develops the primary division.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Quantity is an accident admitting division in imagination through itself. It is first divided into **continuous** and **discrete** quantity.
sourceEvidence.quote: Quantity is an accident admitting division in imagination through itself.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Quantity is divided in its primary division into continuous and discrete.
destinationEvidence.quote: Quantity is divided in its primary division into continuous and discrete.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya gives a separate treatment to divisibility, measurement, equality, and inequality listed together in Bidāya.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Quantity also has characteristic properties. First, its species do not stand in the relation of contraries, because they do not occur in one common subject in the way contraries require. Second, it admits division in imagination, as shown. Third, quantity has something by which it can be measured through repeated subtraction or counting. For discrete quantity the unit is the first measure of all numbers, while certain numbers measure others: two measures four, three measures nine. In continuous quantity a part measures the whole. Fourth, equality and inequality belong properly to quantity and are attributed to other things through quantity.
sourceEvidence.quote: Quantity also has characteristic properties. First, its species do not stand in the relation of contraries, because they do not occur in one common subject in the way contraries require. Second, it admits division in imagination, as shown. Third, quantity has something by which it can be measured through repeated subtraction or counting.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: It was indicated earlier that among the properties of quantity are equality and inequality; division, externally as in number or in the imagination as in other quantities; and the presence within it of a measure that measures it. They have also set out other judgments.
destinationEvidence.quote: It was indicated earlier that among the properties of quantity are equality and inequality; division, externally as in number or in the imagination as in other quantities; and the presence within it of a measure that measures it.

bidayaMapping.topic: the definition and primary divisions of quality
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya explains the exclusions built into the description of quality and then treats its kinds separately.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: Quality is an accident which, considered in itself, does not admit division or relation. The Peripatetic classification distinguishes four primary kinds.
sourceEvidence.quote: Quality is an accident which, considered in itself, does not admit division or relation.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: They define quality as an accident that, through itself, admits neither division nor relation. “Accident” excludes that which is necessary through itself and excludes substance. The qualification “does not admit division” excludes quantity, while “does not admit relation” excludes the seven relational categories. “Through itself” includes that to which division or relation belongs incidentally.
destinationEvidence.quote: They define quality as an accident that, through itself, admits neither division nor relation.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya expands the introductory class of sensible qualities by investigating their operation and sensory divisions.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Fourth**, qualities apprehended through the five external senses. If these pass quickly, like the redness of embarrassment or the pallor of fear, they are called *affections* (infiʿālāt). If relatively stable, like the yellowness of gold and the sweetness of honey, they are called *affective qualities* (infiʿāliyyāt).
sourceEvidence.quote: **Fourth**, qualities apprehended through the five external senses.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: One of the properties of sensible qualities is that they act by assimilation—that is, by making another thing resemble themselves. Heat makes what adjoins it hot, and blackness, for example, casts its image, that is, its likeness, upon the eye.
destinationEvidence.quote: One of the properties of sensible qualities is that they act by assimilation—that is, by making another thing resemble themselves.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both distinguish features such as shape, straightness, and evenness from quantity itself.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Second**, qualities specific to quantities: straightness, curvature, and shape in continuous quantities, and evenness and oddness in discrete numbers.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Second**, qualities specific to quantities: straightness, curvature, and shape in continuous quantities, and evenness and oddness in discrete numbers.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: These are qualities that occur in a body through its quantity: quantity is characterized by them first, and the body is then characterized by them on account of its quantity. Examples are circularity in a line and evenness in a number.
destinationEvidence.quote: These are qualities that occur in a body through its quantity: quantity is characterized by them first, and the body is then characterized by them on account of its quantity.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops Bidāya’s powers and non-powers as bodily preparedness directed toward an external affection.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Third**, dispositional qualities, called *powers and non-powers*. These include a strong disposition to undergo change, such as softness, and a strong disposition not to undergo it, such as hardness. Disposition inhering in matter generally should also be included here. The relation of disposition to substantial potency, which is matter, resembles the relation of mathematical body—the actuality of three-dimensional magnitude—to natural body, which is receptive to it.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Third**, dispositional qualities, called *powers and non-powers*.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The meaning common to them—which has the standing of a species in relation to quality in general and of a genus in relation to their particular species—is an intense bodily preparedness directed toward something external: that is, a preparedness by which the occurrence of something from outside is favored.
destinationEvidence.quote: The meaning common to them—which has the standing of a species in relation to quality in general and of a genus in relation to their particular species—is an intense bodily preparedness directed toward something external: that is, a preparedness by which the occurrence of something from outside is favored.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Bidāya lists psychic qualities; Nihāya investigates their division into passing states and established habits.
bidayaMapping.caution: The category of a psychic quality is not identical with the represented object’s mental existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **First**, psychic qualities, such as knowledge, will, cowardice, courage, despair, and hope.
sourceEvidence.quote: **First**, psychic qualities, such as knowledge, will, cowardice, courage, despair, and hope.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: A psychic quality is, as the Shaykh says, “that which is not connected with bodies in general.” If it is not firmly established, it is called a “state”; if it is firmly established, it is called a “habit.” Since the relation between a state and a habit is that of weakness and intensity, and since they count the two degrees of weakness and intensity as two different species, their position entails counting a state as different from a habit both in species and in existence.
destinationEvidence.quote: A psychic quality is, as the Shaykh says, “that which is not connected with bodies in general.” If it is not firmly established, it is called a “state”; if it is firmly established, it is called a “habit.” Since the relation between a state and a habit is that of weakness and intensity, and since they count the two

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya clarifies why relational categories are configurations grounded in relations, rather than the bare dependent connections themselves.
bidayaMapping.caution: Categorial relation has a quiddity; pure connective existence does not.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Relation** (iḍāfa) is the determination arising from a reciprocal reference between two things. A bare relation in one direction does not yet amount to a categorial relation. Rather, the thing is considered as referred to something that is itself referred back to it—for example, a father considered as father of this child, while the child is considered as child of this father.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Relation** (iḍāfa) is the determination arising from a reciprocal reference between two things.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: You have learned that seven of the categories are relational accidents: relation, where, when, position, possession, acting, and being acted upon. Their being relational means that they are configurations subsisting in their subjects on account of relations present in them. It does not mean that these categories are identical with those existential relations. For you learned in the discussion of dependent and independent existence that a relation is a bond existing in another, with no independence whatever: it is neither predicated of anything nor has anything predicated of it. It therefore has no quiddity, since a quiddity is what is said of a thing in answer to “What is it?” Categories are generic quiddities. Thus a relation is neither a category nor something falling under a category.
destinationEvidence.quote: You have learned that seven of the categories are relational accidents: relation, where, when, position, possession, acting, and being acted upon.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the determination a body acquires through its relation to place.
bidayaMapping.caution: Nihāya VI.17 argues for its distinction from position, but IX.7 later expresses doubt about its independent category status; Bidāya X.10 also raises that qualification.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Where** is the determination arising from a thing's relation to place.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Where** is the determination arising from a thing's relation to place.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Where is a configuration acquired by a body through its relation to place.
destinationEvidence.quote: Where is a configuration acquired by a body through its relation to place.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the determination acquired through relation to time.
bidayaMapping.caution: The category of when is distinguished from time as the measure of motion.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **When** is the determination arising from a thing's relation to time. Being ‘in time’ includes being extended through time, as movements are, and being at its boundary, the instant, as are instantaneous occurrences such as contact, separation, and connection. It also includes being spread across time in the manner of traversing motion or being related to time without such continuous traversal, as in intermediate motion.
sourceEvidence.quote: **When** is the determination arising from a thing's relation to time.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: When is the configuration acquired by a thing through its relation to time.
destinationEvidence.quote: When is the configuration acquired by a thing through its relation to time.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both connect position with relations among parts and of the whole to its surroundings.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Position** is the determination arising from relations of a thing's parts to one another and of the whole to the exterior. Standing, for instance, results from a definite ordering of the limbs, with the head above and the feet below.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Position** is the determination arising from relations of a thing's parts to one another and of the whole to the exterior.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: Position is the configuration that a thing acquires from the relation of some of its parts to others and of the whole to what is external, as in the configurations of standing, sitting, lying on one’s back, and lying face down.
destinationEvidence.quote: Position is the configuration that a thing acquires from the relation of some of its parts to others and of the whole to what is external, as in the configurations of standing, sitting, lying on one’s back, and lying face down.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Both explain possession through an encompassing thing moving with what it encompasses.
bidayaMapping.caution: This category is not the opposition of possession and privation, nor a legal theory of ownership.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Having** (or the category of possession) is the state resulting when one thing surrounds another and the surrounding thing moves when the surrounded thing moves. The enclosure may be complete, as with being wrapped in a cloak, or partial, as with wearing a shirt or shoes.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Having** (or the category of possession) is the state resulting when one thing surrounds another and the surrounding thing moves when the surrounded thing moves.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: This is also called “ownership.” It is the configuration arising from one thing’s encompassing another in such a way that the encompassing thing moves when the encompassed thing moves.
destinationEvidence.quote: This is also called “ownership.” It is the configuration arising from one thing’s encompassing another in such a way that the encompassing thing moves when the encompassed thing moves.

bidayaMapping.topic: the categories of acting and being acted upon
bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the nonstable configurations of an agent and a recipient during an ongoing process.
bidayaMapping.caution: These categorial processes do not cover every instance of metaphysical efficient causation.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: **Acting** is the determination arising in an agent through its affecting another while it acts, as the condition of what heats something while the heating is occurring.
sourceEvidence.quote: **Acting** is the determination arising in an agent through its affecting another while it acts, as the condition of what heats something while the heating is occurring.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: The first is a nonstable configuration arising in an agent from its producing an effect for as long as it produces that effect, as in the heating performed by what heats for as long as it heats, or the cooling performed by what cools for as long as it cools.
destinationEvidence.quote: The first is a nonstable configuration arising in an agent from its producing an effect for as long as it produces that effect, as in the heating performed by what heats for as long as it heats, or the cooling performed by what cools for as long as it cools.

bidayaMapping.comparison: Nihāya develops the same starting point: the effect depends on another existent, and causal efficacy concerns existence.

sourceEvidence.paragraphText: This dependence must be upon an *existent* other, since the non-existent as non-existent has no thingness. The existent upon which the effect thus depends is called a *cause* (ʿilla), and the dependent thing in its existence an *effect* (maʿlūl).
sourceEvidence.quote: This dependence must be upon an *existent* other, since the non-existent as non-existent has no thingness.

destinationEvidence.paragraphText: It was established earlier that quiddity, considered in itself, is neither existent nor nonexistent. Its relation to existence and nonexistence is therefore equal. For either side to prevail for it, it needs something other than itself, external to its essence. Sound reason declares it impossible that either side should prevail without a determinant, whether from its own essence or from something else. You also learned earlier that saying that it needs something else for its nonexistence involves a certain figurative usage. What this really means is that the absence of the other thing needed for its existence is inseparable from the absence of its existence, because its existence depends on the existence of that other thing. Plainly, this dependence is upon the existence of the other thing, since what is nonexistent has no reality as a thing.
